title: Mal Evans dies | 1976
content:
The Beatles’ former roadie Mal Evans died on 4 January 1976, at the age of 40.

Evans had written his last will and testament the day before. The document was witnessed by his girlfriend Fran Hughes, with whom he was renting a motel apartment at 8122 West 4th Street in Los Angeles.

In the afternoon of 4 January, Evans spoke to Ken Mansfield, Apple Records’ former US manager. Mansfield was preparing to leave for the Billboard Music Awards, where he represented country star Jessi Colter.

Evans told Mansfield that he had recently spoken to Paul McCartney, finished writing his memoir, and that “everything’s really great”. Despite his apparent euphoria, Mansfield detected a sadness in Evans’ words, and asked him: “Mal, are you sure everything’s OK? Come on, Mal. Something’s wrong, and we need to talk.”

Because Mansfield was due at the Billboard event, they arranged to have brunch the following morning on Hollywood Boulevard.

Evans grew despondent that afternoon, looking at photographs of his children and crying. At one point he went upstairs and, upon his return, told Hughes that he had taken a whole bottle of Valium. “I can’t have my children,” he told her. “They are dead to me, and I want to die.”

She called Laura Gross, a journalist friend, who was unable to help. She then called John Hoernle, the co-author of Evans’ autobiography. Hoernle recognised Evans’s fragile mental state and immediately set off, arriving at the motel 30 minutes later.

As he entered, Fran was persuading Evans to go upstairs to bed, while her daughter Jody was asleep in the back bedroom. Hoernle followed them into the bedroom. Evans told Hoernle, “Please make sure you and Joanne [Lenard] finish the book,” later describing him as “really doped up and groggy.”

Evans picked up a Winchester rifle, which was loaded with four rounds. The alarmed Hoernle went downstairs while Hughes attempted to persuade Evans to put the gun down. A struggle followed, with Hughes telling Evans, “If you don’t give me that gun now, I’m going to call the police.” He looked her in the eye and said, “Franny, please call the police.”

Hughes called the LAPD, and officers David Krempa and Todd Herman arrived within minutes. She told them, “My old man has a gun and has taken Valium and is really screwed up.”

Krempa and Herman prepared to enter the property, and were joined by fellow officers Robert Brannon and Michael Simonsen. All drew revolvers except for Krempa, who had a shotgun. Hughes and Hoernle remained outside in the front yard.

The master bedroom door was closed, so the officers demanded that Evans walk out with his hands up. After receiving no answer, they continued up the stairs to the doorway. Krempa set his shotgun down, concerned at the proximity to Jody’s bedroom.

Herman kicked the door open. The officers saw Evans sitting on the floor with his legs stretched out in front of him. He was holding the rifle with the barrel aimed towards the floor. Herman repeatedly ordered him to drop the gun. Evans eventually looked up at the officers and told them: “No. Blow my head off.”

Evans then raised the rifle towards his shoulder, as if to take aim. Krempa and Brannon fired six shots, four of which hit Evans. He was killed instantly.

It was so crazy, so crazy. Mal was a big loveable bear of a roadie; he would go over the top occasionally, but we all knew him and never had any problems. The LAPD weren’t so fortunate. They were just told that he was upstairs with a shotgun and so they ran up, kicked the door in and shot him. His girlfriend had told them, ‘He’s a bit moody and he’s got some downers.’ Had I been there I would have been able to say, ‘Mal, don’t be silly.’ In fact, any of his friends could have talked him out of it without any sweat, because he was not a nutter. But his girlfriend – she was an LA girl – didn’t know him that well. She should not have rung the cops, but that’s the way it goes… a thump on the door, ‘Where is he? Where’s the assailant Bang, bang, bang. They don’t ask questions, they shoot first.
Paul McCartney
Anthology

At the sound of the gunshots, more police officers outside ordered Hughes and Hoernle to take cover. An ambulance had been waiting nearby on Fourth Street, following the call to the emergency services about a potential suicide.

Jody was brought out of the apartment unharmed, and reunited with her mother. She had slept throughout the incident. She was left with neighbours while Hughes was taken in for police questioning as a material witness.

Following a subsequent investigation, the LAPD determined that the shooting was a “justifiable homicide”. However, an internal review board recommended remediation for the officers involved, an acknowledgement that more caution should have been exercised. The Shooting Review Board report claimed that the police “should have taken more time to assess the situation properly”, and that the decision to enter the property “placed the officers in a position of disadvantage and could have resulted in an officer being killed or seriously injured.”

Evans’s body was cremated at Forest Lawn cemetery in Los Angeles on 7 January 1976.

I went down to Forest Lawn and said I was sort of new at this, but what happens next? I said that I thought he should be cremated because it’s cheaper for the family. So they cremated him and as I was walking out, I said, ‘By the way, how do you get these ashes to London?’ They said, ‘Well, we have these cardboard cylinders.’ I said, ‘You’d send a mother the remains of her son in a cardboard box? What else do you have?’ And they said, ‘We have this beautiful diamond-encrusted ruby old … We have this brass thing here with emeralds.’ So I picked out a nice sort of shape that looked expensive and was appropriate, and sent that to London.
Harry Nilsson

The ashes were flown to England, but went missing for several weeks before eventually being found on a warehouse shelf at Heathrow Airport.

A memorial service, attended by Evans’ family, was held in February 1976 at South West Middlesex Crematorium. The former Beatles did not attend, but George Harrison arranged for Evans’ family to receive £5,000 to cover expenses.

On 26 February, a second memorial service was held at the Church of All Hallows in Allerton, Liverpool. Among those in attendance were George Martin and Apple’s Neil Aspinall.
